'''X-ray [[absorption spectroscopy]]''' (XAS) is a set of advanced techniques used for probing the local environment of matter at atomic level and its electronic structure.<ref>{{Citation|chapter=Introduction to X-Ray Absorption Fine Structure (XAFS)|date=2017-11-24|chapter-url=https://doi-org.ezproxy1.library.usyd.edu.au/10.1002/9781118676165.ch1|title=X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy for the Chemical and Materials Sciences|pages=1–8|place=Chichester, UK|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd|doi=10.1002/9781118676165.ch1|isbn=978-1-118-67616-5|access-date=2020-09-28|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> The experiments require access to [[synchrotron radiation]] facilities for their intense and tunable [[X-ray]] beams. Samples can be in the gas phase, solutions, or solids.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yano J, Yachandra VK | title = X-ray absorption spectroscopy | journal = Photosynthesis Research | volume = 102 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 241–54 | date = 2009-08-04 | pmid = 19653117 | pmc = 2777224 | doi = 10.1007/s11120-009-9473-8 | bibcode = 2009PhoRe.102..241Y | url = }}</ref>

== Background ==
XAS data are obtained by tuning the [[photon]] energy,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Popmintchev|first1=Dimitar|last2=Galloway|first2=Benjamin R.|last3=Chen|first3=Ming-Chang|last4=Dollar|first4=Franklin|last5=Mancuso|first5=Christopher A.|last6=Hankla|first6=Amelia|last7=Miaja-Avila|first7=Luis|last8=O'Neil|first8=Galen|last9=Shaw|first9=Justin M.|last10=Fan|first10=Guangyu|last11=Ališauskas|first11=Skirmantas|date=2018-03-01|title=Near- and Extended-Edge X-Ray-Absorption Fine-Structure Spectroscopy Using Ultrafast Coherent High-Order Harmonic Supercontinua|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=120|issue=9|article-number=093002|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.120.093002|pmid=29547333|bibcode=2018PhRvL.120i3002P |issn=0031-9007|doi-access=free|hdl=20.500.12708/17936|hdl-access=free}}</ref> using a crystalline monochromator, to a range where [[core electron]]s can be excited (0.1-100 keV). The edges are, in part, named by which core electron is excited: the [[principal quantum number]]s n = 1, 2, and 3, correspond to the K-, L-, and M-edges, respectively.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Kelly SD, Hesterberg D, Ravel B | chapter = Analysis of Soils and Minerals Using X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy|date=2015| chapter-url=https://acsess.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2136/sssabookser5.5.c14| title = Methods of Soil Analysis Part 5—Mineralogical Methods| series = SSSA Book Series|pages=387–463|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd|language=en|doi=10.2136/sssabookser5.5.c14|isbn=978-0-89118-857-5|access-date=2020-09-24}}</ref> For instance, excitation of a 1s electron occurs at the [[metal K-edge|K-edge]], while excitation of a 2s or 2p electron occurs at an [[metal L-edge|L-edge]] (Figure 1).

There are three main regions found on a spectrum generated by XAS data, which are then thought of as separate spectroscopic techniques (Figure 2):
# The ''absorption threshold'' determined by the transition to the lowest unoccupied states: {{ordered list
 | list-style-type=lower-alpha
 | the states at the [[Fermi level]] in metals giving a "rising edge" with an [[arc tangent]] shape; 
 | the [[exciton|bound core excitons]] in insulators with a [[Cauchy distribution|Lorentzian]]  line-shape (they occur in a pre-edge region at energies lower than the transitions to the lowest unoccupied level);
 }} 
# The X-ray absorption near-edge structure ([[XANES]]), introduced in 1980 and later in 1983 and also called NEXAFS (near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure), which are dominated by core transitions to quasi bound states (multiple scattering resonances) for photoelectrons with kinetic energy in the range from 10 to 150 eV above the chemical potential, called "shape resonances" in molecular spectra since they are due to final states of short life-time degenerate with the continuum with the Fano line-shape. In this range, multi-electron excitations and many-body final states in strongly correlated systems are relevant; 
# In the high kinetic energy range of the photoelectron, the scattering cross-section with neighbor atoms is weak, and the absorption spectra are dominated by [[EXAFS]] (extended X-ray absorption fine structure), where the scattering of the ejected [[photoelectron]] of neighboring atoms can be approximated by single scattering events. In 1985, it was shown that multiple scattering theory can be used to interpret both [[XANES]] and [[EXAFS]]; therefore, the experimental analysis focusing on both regions is now called [[XAFS]].

XAS is a type of [[absorption spectroscopy]] from a core initial state with a well-defined symmetry; therefore, the quantum mechanical [[selection rules]] select the symmetry of the final states in the continuum, which are usually a mixture of multiple components. The most intense features are due to electric-dipole allowed transitions (i.e. ''Δℓ'' = ± 1) to unoccupied final states. For example, the most intense features of a K-edge are due to core transitions from 1s → p-like final states, while the most intense features of the L<sub>3</sub>-edge are due to 2p → d-like final states.

XAS methodology can be broadly divided into four experimental categories that can yield complementary results: [[metal K-edge]], [[metal L-edge]], [[ligand K-edge]], and EXAFS.

The most obvious means of mapping heterogeneous samples beyond x-ray absorption contrast is through elemental analysis by x-ray fluorescence, similar to EDX methods in electron microscopy.<ref>{{Cite book|author=Evans, John |title=X-ray absorption spectroscopy for the chemical and materials sciences|date=23 November 2017|isbn=978-1-118-67617-2|edition=First |location=Hoboken, NJ|oclc=989811256}}</ref>

== Applications ==
XAS is a technique used in various scientific fields, including [[Molecular physics|molecular]] and [[condensed matter physics]],<ref>Tangcharoen, T., Klysubun, W., Kongmark, C., & Pecharapa, W. (2014). Synchrotron X‐ray absorption spectroscopy and magnetic characteristics studies of metal ferrites (metal = Ni, Mn, Cu) synthesized by sol–gel auto‐combustion method. Physica Status Solidi A, 211(8), 1903-1911.https://doi.org/10.1002/pssa.201330477</ref><ref>Tangcharoen, Thanit, Wantana Klysubun, and Chanapa Kongmark. "Synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy and cation distribution studies of NiAl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, CuAl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, and ZnAl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> nanoparticles synthesized by sol-gel auto combustion method." Journal of Molecular Structure 1182 (2019): 219-229.https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molstruc.2019.01.049</ref><ref>Rawat, Pankaj Singh, R. C. Srivastava, Gagan Dixit, and K. Asokan. "Structural, functional and magnetic ordering modifications in graphene oxide and graphite by 100 MeV gold ion irradiation." Vacuum 182 (2020): 109700. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vacuum.2020.109700</ref> [[materials science and engineering]], [[chemistry]], [[earth science]], and [[biology]]. In particular, its unique sensitivity to the local structure, as compared to [[x-ray diffraction]], has been exploited for studying:

* [[Amorphous solid]]s and [[liquid]] systems
* [[Solid solution]]s
* [[Doping (semiconductor)|Doping]] and [[ion implantation]] materials for [[electronics]]
* Local distortions of [[crystal structure|crystal lattices]]
* [[Organometallic chemistry|Organometallic compounds]]
* [[Metalloproteins]]
* [[Cluster chemistry|Metal clusters]]
* [[Catalysis]]
* Vibrational dynamics<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ljungberg |first1=Mathias |title=Vibrational effects in x-ray absorption and resonant inelastic x-ray scattering using a semiclassical scheme |journal=Physical Review B |date=December 2017 |volume=96 |issue=21 |article-number=214302 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.96.214302 |arxiv=1709.06786 |bibcode=2017PhRvB..96u4302L |s2cid=119210376 |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.96.214302 |access-date=21 April 2023}}</ref>
* [[Ion]]s in [[Solution (chemistry)|solution]]s
* Speciation of elements
* [[Liquid water]] and aqueous solutions
* Used to detect bone fractures
* Used to determine the concentration of any liquid in any tank
